question: What is the main goal of providing nutrition care for patients in the hospital?

options.B: Reducing the cost of hospital food services
options.C: Replacing the need for doctor-ordered diets
options.D: Ensuring patients gain weight during every stay

explanation: Great job! Good nutrition keeps the body strong so it can fight off infections and heal wounds faster.

question: Why are patients in the hospital often at a high risk for poor nutrition?

options.A: Patients lose interest in healthy eating habits
options.B: Too many high-calorie snacks are available
options.C: Illness, frequent fasting, and poor appetite

explanation: Spot on! Being sick, missing meals for lab tests, and just feeling unwell can easily kill a patient's appetite.

question: When a patient is admitted to the ward, who usually does the first nutritional screening?
explanation: That's right! As the nurse admitting the patient, you do the initial check to see if they need a special dietary review.

question: A newly admitted patient is too weak to stand on the weighing scale. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Record the weight from their visit five years ago
options.B: Skip the weight measurement until discharge
options.C: Use a bed scale or lift scale for an accurate baseline
options.D: Ask a family member to guess the patient's weight

explanation: Spot on! An accurate baseline weight is key for tracking fluid balance and nutrition, so specialized scales are a lifesaver.

question: Which specialist checks if a patient can swallow safely and recommends the right food textures?
explanation: Correct! Speech therapists are experts at testing swallow safety and helping prevent dangerous choking or aspiration.

question: Why is the bedside nurse considered the central link in the healthcare nutrition team?

options.A: They have legal power to prescribe diets
options.B: They do all formal nutrition assessments alone
options.C: They observe daily intake and update the team
options.D: They are the only ones allowed to serve food

explanation: You got it! Because we are always at the bedside, we notice what the patient eats and share that info with the doctors and dietitians.

question: What is the best position for a patient who needs help with eating?

options.A: Flat on the back with neck extended
options.C: Lying on the left side with knees bent

explanation: Correct! Sitting upright uses gravity to protect the airway and keeps food safely going down instead of into the lungs.

question: What should the nurse do before bringing a meal tray to a patient who needs feeding help?

options.A: Restrict all fluids until the meal is finished
options.B: Clear the bedside table and clean your hands
options.C: Give a sleeping pill to calm them down
options.D: Insist that family members feed every meal

explanation: Spot on! Basic hygiene and a clean, clutter-free space make mealtime safe and much more inviting.

question: How do nurses usually record how much of a meal a patient actually ate in the chart?

options.A: Counting every individual grain of rice
options.B: Taking a photo of the tray after eating
options.C: Weighing food scraps on a gram scale
options.D: Percentage estimation of the meal eaten

explanation: That's right! We estimate intake in quarters (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) to quickly track how much nourishment they got.

question: A patient's tray is empty, but you suspect they didn't eat. What might have happened?

options.A: Food may have been eaten by a visitor or spilled
options.B: Dietary intake only counts if a dietitian sees it
options.C: The kitchen staff forgot to put food on the plate
options.D: The patient's metabolism is moving too fast

explanation: Correct! An empty tray doesn't guarantee the patient ate the food. Always double-check before charting their intake.

question: What is the minimum head-of-bed elevation for a patient on continuous tube feeding?
explanation: Spot on! Keeping the head of the bed raised prevents the formula from flowing backward into the lungs.

question: Why must strict sterile technique be used when handling parenteral nutrition (IV feeding) lines?

options.A: Sterile technique stops the plastic from melting
options.B: Central lines connect to the digestive tract
options.C: The high nutrient content breeds bacteria fast
options.D: IV solutions contain live active bacteria

explanation: That's correct! Because these IV solutions are packed with sugars and proteins, germs love to grow in them, risking serious infection.

question: How should a nurse best approach diet education for a patient going home with a new health condition?

options.A: Assume they already know basics from TV
options.B: Focus only on foods they cannot eat
options.C: Tailor teaching to their lifestyle and culture
options.D: Hand out a complex medical textbook to read

explanation: You got it! Teaching works best when it fits the patient's daily life, culture, and personal background.

question: A patient with high blood pressure struggles with low-sodium guidelines. What is the best teaching strategy?

options.A: Provide a list of Latin names for salty ingredients
options.B: Explain the chemical structure of sodium chloride
options.C: Show them how to read grocery food labels
options.D: Tell them to stop eating outside food forever

explanation: Spot on! Teaching practical skills like reading labels empowers patients to make healthy choices when shopping on their own.

question: Which clinical sign do nurses commonly track to check a patient's nutrition progress over time?
explanation: Correct! Tracking weight changes over time gives us a clear picture of whether our nutrition plan is working.

question: Why is detailed nursing documentation of a patient's nutrition care so important?

options.A: It guarantees the hospital gets zero complaints
options.B: It ensures continuity of care and creates a permanent record
options.C: It lets nurses prescribe their own diet orders
options.D: It replaces the need to give verbal shift handovers

explanation: Well done! Good charting keeps every nurse and team member on the same page across different shifts.
